compute.body: Semiconductor and electronic-component output growth accelerated materially to 19.9%, while capacity utilization rose to 76.5%. Computer and peripheral-equipment output growth slowed materially to 6.5%, and utilization edged down to 81.3%. Both segments are still expanding, but the latest acceleration is concentrated in semiconductors.
compute.headline: Semiconductor production accelerates as computer-equipment growth cools

data_center.body: Available records list 1,556 data-center sites in development, about half of the 3,068 operating sites, and separately identify 894 active pipeline sites. The Texas Tribune reported that TCEQ shut down its permit-filing system amid a data-center dispute. The shutdown is a fresh administrative interruption, but it does not establish that the broader pipeline is shrinking.
data_center.headline: A Texas permit-system shutdown adds uncertainty to a large data-center pipeline

economic_impact.body: Nonfarm-business productivity grew 2.2% alongside a 2.5% increase in real output, while real hourly compensation rose 0.6%. Unit labor costs increased 1.4%. The pattern shows broad productivity gains without a comparable rise in real hourly compensation, but it does not identify the source of those gains. Axios reported skepticism that AI is yet adding much to productivity. That report is consistent with the attribution problem in the aggregate data, not proof that AI has had no effect.
economic_impact.headline: Productivity growth outpaces real compensation, but AI’s contribution remains unclear

finance.body: The Chicago Fed NFCI stands at -0.49 after rising 0.04 over three months. Lender strain increased slightly to 17.4, and corporate bond-market distress edged up to 0.25. These measures point in the same direction at the margin, but not with the same intensity. The Financial Times reported a surge in default-insurance trading tied to AI debt concerns, while Morningstar reported a $40 billion GPU leasing deal involving SpaceX and private-credit firms. The reports show that very large AI-related financing and greater trading in credit protection can occur at the same time; they do not establish broad credit deterioration by themselves.
finance.headline: Credit indicators edge toward greater strain even as private credit funds a large GPU deal

macro.body: AI equity performance has strengthened across more than one measure. The AI Equity Index rose materially to 38.2, the median one-year return reached 13.8%, and the equal-weight return edged up to 21.3%. Investor’s Business Daily reported that an Nvidia partner surged after strong earnings and guidance, while Reuters highlighted Anthropic’s combination of rapid sales growth and steep losses ahead of an IPO. Investors are still rewarding AI exposure, but those examples underscore that supplier earnings and model-company economics remain very different propositions. The financing system can support very large commitments, though its direction has become somewhat less favorable. The Chicago Fed NFCI rose 0.04 over three months to -0.49, while lender strain and corporate bond distress both edged higher. Morningstar reported a $40 billion GPU leasing deal involving SpaceX and private credit, and the Financial Times reported a surge in default-insurance trading amid AI debt concerns. Large financing capacity and increased credit hedging are visible at the same time; neither report demonstrates system-wide distress. Power remains the clearest physical execution issue. Commercial electricity demand is growing 3.5%, faster than total retail demand at 1.8%, and retail prices are up 5.1%. Supply pipelines look large on separate measures: net planned generation additions total 227.6 GW, and active interconnection queues contain 2,061 GW. Yet only 24.2% of the queue is in executed-agreement or construction stages, and 13% of the 2000–2020 cohort reached operation. Utility Dive’s report on Google’s virtual power plant in PJM shows one company pursuing another route while new generation works through the pipeline. The central distinction remains between announced capacity and power that can actually serve load. The macroeconomic return remains harder to identify than the investment itself. Nonfarm-business productivity grew 2.2% and real output 2.5%, but real hourly compensation rose 0.6% and unit labor costs 1.4%. Business adoption is still partial: 24.6% report current AI use and 28.6% expect to use it within six months, compared with 60.8% of adults ages 18–64 reporting some generative-AI use. These figures show broad consumer use and narrower business deployment, but they cannot isolate AI’s contribution to productivity or compensation.
macro.headline: AI equity gains strengthen as debt exposure and power-delivery risk come into clearer view

market.body: The AI Equity Index rose materially to 38.2, while the median one-year return climbed to 13.8% and the equal-weight return edged up to 21.3%. Average sector trading pressure slipped slightly to 47.9, so the stronger trailing performance has not coincided with more intense trading pressure. Investor’s Business Daily reported that an Nvidia partner rallied after strong earnings and guidance; Reuters separately described Anthropic’s rapid sales growth and steep losses as a test for its IPO. The contrast illustrates why strong demand for AI exposure can coexist with sharply different underlying economics.
market.headline: AI equity gains strengthen beyond the headline index

editorial_briefing.style_reference: AI Macro is a research platform that examines the development of the U.S. AI economy from capital investment and physical construction through deployment, adoption, and economic results. It uses publicly available data to relate corporate and market activity to the physical systems required to support the buildout. It evaluates the extent to which that investment produces durable economic value and how its effects are transmitted through the broader U.S. economy.

Investment remains strong, but financing risks and economy-wide effects are less settled

paragraphs.text: Investment remains the clearest current signal. Information-processing investment growth accelerated materially to 20.6%, semiconductor and electronic-component output grew 19.9%, and available records list 1,556 data-center sites in development—about half the operating count. The AI Equity Index also rose materially to 40.8, although the median covered-company return eased to 13.4%. These measures cover different parts of the technology and infrastructure cycle, but they show a large buildout with continued market support rather than uniform gains.

Financing capacity is less uniform. Operating cash flow covers current CapEx by 1.39 times, but cash reserves equal 0.92 years of CapEx. Borrower strain at 26.1 exceeds lender strain at 17.4. Reuters reported that Moody’s sees AI financing driving private-credit growth as refinancing risks rise. The aggregate internal-funding position does not describe every project or remove rollover risk where outside capital is required.

The economy-wide payoff remains harder to assign. Nonfarm-business productivity grew 2.2% and real output 2.5%, while real hourly compensation rose 0.6%. Current AI use is reported by 24.6% of businesses, compared with 28.6% expecting use within six months. These data show positive broad gains and incomplete business diffusion, but they cannot establish how much AI contributed. The buildout is easier to measure than its effect on productivity and pay.

Information-processing investment growth accelerated materially to 20.6%, semiconductor and electronic-component output grew 19.9%, and available records list 1,556 data-center sites in development—about half the operating count. The AI Equity Index also rose materially to 40.8, although the median covered-company return eased to 13.4%. These measures cover different parts of the technology and infrastructure cycle, but they show a large buildout with continued market support rather than uniform gains.

Financing capacity is less uniform. Operating cash flow covers current CapEx by 1.39 times, but cash reserves equal 0.92 years of CapEx. Borrower strain at 26.1 exceeds lender strain at 17.4. Reuters reported that Moody’s sees AI financing driving private-credit growth as refinancing risks rise. The aggregate internal-funding position does not describe every project or remove rollover risk where outside capital is required.

The economy-wide payoff remains harder to assign. Nonfarm-business productivity grew 2.2% and real output 2.5%, while real hourly compensation rose 0.6%. Current AI use is reported by 24.6% of businesses, compared with 28.6% expecting use within six months. These data show positive broad gains and incomplete business diffusion, but they cannot establish how much AI contributed. The buildout is easier to measure than its effect on productivity and pay.
